Isaiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Isaiah prophesied during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.

He has rightly been called the evangelical prophet, because he speaks frequently and at length about the Messiah—his coming and character, his ministry and preaching, his suffering and death, and the extent and lasting nature of his kingdom.

Behind the promised deliverance from Babylon, Isaiah also reveals a far greater deliverance to be accomplished by the Messiah.

He seldom speaks of the nearer rescue without also pointing toward the greater one. Sometimes he becomes so absorbed in the later deliverance that he seems to leave the nearer event behind, speaking at length about the Messiah's person, work, character and kingdom.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe corruptions prevailing among the Jews.1–9Severe censures.10–15Exhortations to repentance.16–20The state of Judah is lamented; with gracious promises of the gospel times.21–31
Judah's widespread corruption (verses 1–9)

Isaiah means the salvation of the Lord, a fitting name for a prophet who speaks so frequently about Jesus the Savior and his salvation.

God's professing people failed to recognize that every comfort and even life itself came from his fatherly kindness.

Many people are equally careless about their souls. Failing to consider truth we already know can harm us as much as not knowing truth we ought to learn.

Wickedness had spread throughout the land.

The prophet pictured the nation as a sick body whose disease threatened death. From foot to head—from the poorest worker to the most powerful ruler—there was no spiritual health.

Guilt and corruption were everywhere, the sorrowful effects of Adam's fall. Henry understands this picture as declaring the total depravity of fallen human nature.

When people refuse to repent, their spiritual wounds remain untreated, and ruin approaches.

Jerusalem stood exposed like the temporary huts built to watch over ripening fruit. Such shelters were familiar in the East.

Yet the Lord preserved a small faithful remnant in the city.

It is because of his mercy that we have not been destroyed.

The evil nature described here exists in each of us. Only Jesus Christ and his sanctifying Spirit can restore our souls to spiritual health.

Sacrifice without repentance is unacceptable (verses 10–15)

Judah's countryside lay desolate and cities had burned. Those judgments moved the people to offer sacrifices.

But they approached worship as though they might pay God to remove punishment while continuing in sin.

Many are willing to surrender expensive offerings who remain unwilling to surrender their sinful practices.

They regard religious forms as good deeds that entitle them to reward.

Yet even the costliest worship is unacceptable without a genuine change of heart and life.

God not only refused such sacrifices; he hated their hypocrisy.

Sin is deeply offensive to him.

If we continue secretly cherishing forbidden sins or reject Christ's salvation, even our prayers become offensive rather than acceptable.

Turn from evil and begin doing good (verses 16–20)

Repentance is not merely sorrow over past actions. Stop practicing evil and begin doing the good God commands.

We must not stand idle when there are duties to fulfill.

The sacrifices prescribed in Moses' law could not of themselves atone even for the nation's outward crimes.

But God has opened a fountain of cleansing, available to sinners of every age and social rank.

Our sins may be like scarlet and crimson, dyed deeply and repeatedly: first in the wool of original corruption, then through the many threads of our own deliberate transgressions.

Even after repeated backsliding, God's pardoning mercy can remove the stain (Psalm 51:7).

Life and death, good and evil, are set before us.

Lord, incline us all to live for your glory.

Zion's corruption and promised redemption (verses 21–31)

Neither a holy city nor a royal capital fulfills its purpose if true religion no longer lives within it.

Impure metal may still resemble silver. Diluted wine may still look like wine. In the same way, outward appearances may conceal spiritual corruption.

People who oppress the vulnerable rather than help them bear grave responsibility.

Human rules and restraints can accomplish something outwardly. But only God can change hearts effectively through his Spirit acting in judgment and renewal.

Sin is the worst form of captivity and slavery.

Henry regards these verses as fitting most fully the redemption of spiritual Zion through Christ's righteousness, death and powerful grace.

The unrepentant face complete ruin. They resemble a tree scorched by heat or a garden without water, quickly ruined in a dry land.

Those who put their trust in idols or human strength will perish.

Even a strong person will become like dry tinder, easily broken and readily set on fire.

When sinners make themselves like stubble and meet God as a consuming fire, nothing can prevent their destruction unless they receive his mercy.
classic_reading:
[Isa.1.1-Isa.1.9]
Isaiah
Isaiah prophesied in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. He has been well called the evangelical prophet, on account of his numerous and full prophesies concerning the coming and character, the ministry and preaching, the sufferings and death of the Messiah, and the extent and continuance of his kingdom. Under the veil of the deliverance from Babylon, Isaiah points to a much greater deliverance, which was to be effected by the Messiah; and seldom does he mention the one, without alluding at the same time to the other; nay, he is often so much enraptured with the prospect of the more distant deliverance, as to lose sight of that which was nearer, and to dwell on the Messiah's person, office, character, and kingdom.
Chapter 1
The corruptions prevailing among the Jews. ( [Isa.1.1-Isa.1.9] Is. 1:1-9) Severe censures. ( [Isa.1.10-Isa.1.15] Is. 1:10-15) Exhortations to repentance. ( [Isa.1.16-Isa.1.20] Is. 1:16-20) The state of Judah is lamented; with gracious promises of the gospel times. ( [Isa.1.21-Isa.1.31] Is. 1:21-31)
Verses 1-9 Isaiah signifies, "The salvation of the Lord;" a very suitable name for this prophet, who prophesies so much of Jesus the Saviour, and his salvation. God's professing people did not know or consider that they owed their lives and comforts to God's fatherly care and kindness. How many are very careless in the affairs of their souls! Not considering what we do know in religion, does us as much harm, as ignorance of what we should know. The wickedness was universal. Here is a comparison taken from a sick and diseased body. The distemper threatens to be mortal. From the sole of the foot even to the head; from the meanest peasant to the greatest peer, there is no soundness, no good principle, no religion, for that is the health of the soul. Nothing but guilt and corruption; the sad effects of Adam's fall. This passage declares the total depravity of human nature. While sin remains unrepented, nothing is done toward healing these wounds, and preventing fatal effects. Jerusalem was exposed and unprotected, like the huts or sheds built up to guard ripening fruits. These are still to be seen in the East, where fruits form a large part of the summer food of the people. But the Lord had a small remnant of pious servants at Jerusalem. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed. The evil nature is in every one of us; only Jesus and his sanctifying Spirit can restore us to spiritual health.
[Isa.1.10-Isa.1.15]
Verses 10-15 Judea was desolate, and their cities burned. This awakened them to bring sacrifices and offerings, as if they would bribe God to remove the punishment, and give them leave to go on in their sin. Many who will readily part with their sacrifices, will not be persuaded to part with their sins. They relied on the mere form as a service deserving a reward. The most costly devotions of wicked people, without thorough reformation of heart and life, cannot be acceptable to God. He not only did not accept them, but he abhorred them. All this shows that sin is very hateful to God. If we allow ourselves in secret sin, or forbidden indulgences; if we reject the salvation of Christ, our very prayers will become abomination.
[Isa.1.16-Isa.1.20]
Verses 16-20 Not only feel sorrow for the sin committed, but break off the practice. We must be doing, not stand idle. We must be doing the good the Lord our God requires. It is plain that the sacrifices of the law could not atone, even for outward national crimes. But, blessed be God, there is a Fountain opened, in which sinners of every age and rank may be cleansed. Though our sins have been as scarlet and crimson, a deep dye, a double dye, first in the wool of original corruption, and afterwards in the many threads of actual transgression; though we have often dipped into sin, by many backslidings; yet pardoning mercy will take out the stain, Ps. 51:7. They should have all the happiness and comfort they could desire. Life and death, good and evil, are set before us. O Lord, incline all of us to live to thy glory.
[Isa.1.21-Isa.1.31]
Verses 21-31 Neither holy cities nor royal ones are faithful to their trust, if religion does not dwell in them. Dross may shine like silver, and the wine that is mixed with water may still have the colour of wine. Those have a great deal to answer for, who do not help the oppressed, but oppress them. Men may do much by outward restraints; but only God works effectually by the influences of his Spirit, as a Spirit of Judgment. Sin is the worst captivity, the worst slavery. The redemption of the spiritual Zion, by the righteousness and death of Christ, and by his powerful grace, most fully accord with what is here meant. Utter ruin is threatened. The Jews should become as a tree when blasted by heat; as a garden without water, which in those hot countries would soon be burned up. Thus shall they be that trust in idols, or in an arm of flesh. Even the strong man shall be as tow; not only soon broken, and pulled to pieces, but easily catching fire. When the sinner has made himself as tow and stubble, and God makes himself as a consuming fire, what can prevent the utter ruin of the sinner?

The nations called to God's light (verses 1–9)

Isaiah foretells the calling of the Gentiles, the spread of the gospel and a still wider proclamation yet to come.

Christians should encourage and strengthen one another.

God teaches his people through his word and Spirit.

Christ advances peace as well as holiness. If every human being were a genuine Christian, war would no longer exist.

But the complete fulfillment of this vision has not yet appeared in the world.

Whatever others do, let us walk in the light of that peace.

When true faith flourishes, people delight in gathering for worship and urge others to join them.

We should be cautious about making those who do not know God our closest guides and companions; we easily imitate the habits of people with whom we spend time.

God does not condemn people simply for owning silver or gold, horses or chariots.

The wrong lies in depending upon possessions and military strength, as though they guaranteed safety, comfort and happiness or as though we could have none without them.

Sin disgraces people of every rank.

Countries that describe themselves as Christian may no longer be filled with literal idols. Yet they can be full of wealth treated as a god.

When people are consumed with their gains and pleasures, they forget or despise God's truth and commandments.

Human pride humbled before the Lord (verses 10–22)

Henry regards the Chaldean conquest of Jerusalem as the first historical judgment in view, during which Jewish idolatry was brought low.

Yet the passage also turns our attention toward the final destruction of Christ's enemies.

People who face God's judgment cannot hide or find safe shelter from it.

The shaking of the earth will terrify those who have attached their hearts to earthly things.

Human arrogance will be brought low, either through God's grace convincing people of pride's evil or through Providence removing the things in which they took pride.

The Lord's day of judgment comes against everything in which sinners place their trust.

Those unwilling to listen to warning and reason may eventually be forced to recognize their danger through terror.

People who make money their god will discover it has become a burden.

Henry also applies this passage to an awakened sinner willing to surrender everything to receive salvation.

The Jews had been inclined to depend on neighboring nations instead of the Lord.

We face the same temptation to depend upon mortal human beings.

Let no person become your ultimate fear or your ultimate hope. Place your hope in the Lord your God.

[Isa.2.1-Isa.2.9]
Chapter 2
The conversion of the Gentiles, Description of the sinfulness of Israel. ( [Isa.2.1-Isa.2.9] Is. 2:1-9) The awful punishment of unbelievers. ( [Isa.2.10-Isa.2.22] Is. 2:10-22)
Verses 1-9 The calling of the Gentiles, the spread of the gospel, and that far more extensive preaching of it yet to come, are foretold. Let Christians strengthen one another, and support one another. It is God who teaches his people, by his word and Spirit. Christ promotes peace, as well as holiness. If all men were real Christians, there could be no war; but nothing answering to these expressions has yet taken place on the earth. Whatever others do, let us walk in the light of this peace. Let us remember that when true religion flourishes, men delight in going up to the house of the Lord, and in urging others to accompany them. Those are in danger who please themselves with strangers to God; for we soon learn to follow the ways of persons whose company we keep. It is not having silver and gold, horses and chariots, that displeases God, but depending upon them, as if we could not be safe, and easy, and happy without them, and could not but be so with them. Sin is a disgrace to the poorest and the lowest. And though lands called Christian are not full of idols, in the literal sense, are they not full of idolized riches? and are not men so busy about their gains and indulgences, that the Lord, his truths, and precepts, are forgotten or despised?
[Isa.2.10-Isa.2.22]
Verses 10-22 The taking of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans seems first meant here, when idolatry among the Jews was done away; but our thoughts are led forward to the destruction of all the enemies of Christ. It is folly for those who are pursued by the wrath of God, to think to hide or shelter themselves from it. The shaking of the earth will be terrible to those who set their affections on things of the earth. Men's haughtiness will be brought down, either by the grace of God convincing them of the evil of pride, or by the providence of God depriving them of all the things they were proud of. The day of the Lord shall be upon those things in which they put their confidence. Those who will not be reasoned out of their sins, sooner or later shall be frightened out of them. Covetous men make money their god; but the time will come when they will feel it as much their burden. This whole passage may be applied to the case of an awakened sinner, ready to leave all that his soul may be saved. The Jews were prone to rely on their heathen neighbours; but they are here called upon to cease from depending on mortal man. We are all prone to the same sin. Then let not man be your fear, let not him be your hope; but let your hope be in the Lord your God. Let us make this our great concern.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe calamities about to come upon the land.1–9The wickedness of the people.10–15The distress of the proud, luxurious women of Zion.16–26
Judah is deprived of its supports (verses 1–9)

God was about to remove every support on which Judah depended.

Jerusalem and the land would become desolate because the people's words and deeds were rebellions against the Lord, even at his holy temple.

When people refuse to rely upon God, he may take away their other sources of security. Then they discover how weak they truly are.

Jesus Christ is the Bread of Life and the Water of Life. If he is our support, we possess a lasting portion that cannot be taken away (John 6:27).

Henry draws three lessons from the threatened judgment.

First, the condition of unrepentant sinners is deeply miserable.

Second, it is the soul that sin most seriously damages.

Third, people who continue in sin bring the evil they suffer upon themselves.

Righteousness and oppression (verses 10–15)

Whether the nation is prosperous or suffering, God's final principle remains unchanged:

It will be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked.

The godly therefore have abundant reason to trust him, and sinners have every reason to repent and return.

The time had come for the Lord to demonstrate his power and call leaders to account for their use of the wealth and authority entrusted to them.

Neglecting the needs of poor people is sinful.

How much more hateful is the conduct of those who first reduce people to poverty and then exploit them!

The pride and luxury of Zion (verses 16–26)

Isaiah warned the women of Zion that suffering would follow their pride and extravagance.

God notices outward vanity, even in dress.

The threatened judgments corresponded to the sins being condemned.

Henry describes repulsive illness as one form such judgment could take.

The precise kind of ornaments worn is not the essential point. Fashions change, and what seems impressive in one age might look absurd in another.

Human nature, however, remains the same.

Wasting time and money on self-display while neglecting faith, generosity and even justice displeases the Lord.

Even people who profess religion sometimes treat excessive luxury and ornamentation as morally harmless. But Henry asks why the Holy Spirit would have directed the prophet to expose it so carefully if it were not a serious evil.

Jerusalem would be conquered and reduced to ruins.

The prophet pictures it as a grieving woman sitting on the ground.

Henry notes a later Roman medal celebrating Jerusalem's destruction with a similar image of a seated, mourning woman.

Whenever sin is deliberately sheltered inside a city's walls, grief and mourning are likely to arrive at its gates.

[Isa.3.1-Isa.3.9]

The calamities about to come upon the land. ( [Isa.3.1-Isa.3.9] Is. 3:1-9) The wickedness of the people. ( [Isa.3.10-Isa.3.15] Is. 3:10-15) The distress of the proud, luxurious women of Zion. ( [Isa.3.16-Isa.3.26] Is. 3:16-26)
Verses 1-9 God was about to deprive Judah of every stay and support. The city and the land were to be made desolate, because their words and works had been rebellious against the Lord; even at his holy temple. If men do not stay themselves upon God, he will soon remove all other supports, and then they must sink. Christ is the Bread of life and the Water of life; if he be our Stay, we shall find that is a good part not to be taken away, John 6:27. Here note, 1. That the condition of sinners is exceedingly woful. 2. It is the soul that is damaged by sin. 3. Whatever evil befals sinners, be sure that they bring it on themselves.
[Isa.3.10-Isa.3.15]
Verses 10-15 The rule was certain; however there might be national prosperity or trouble, it would be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked. Blessed be God, there is abundant encouragement to the righteous to trust in him, and for sinners to repent and return to him. It was time for the Lord to show his might. He will call men to a strict account for all the wealth and power intrusted to and abused by them. If it is sinful to disregard the necessities of the poor, how odious and wicked a part do they act, who bring men into poverty, and then oppress them!
[Isa.3.16-Isa.3.26]
Verses 16-26 The prophet reproves and warns the daughters of Zion of the sufferings coming upon them. Let them know that God notices the folly and vanity of proud women, even of their dress. The punishments threatened answered the sin. Loathsome diseases often are the just punishment of pride. It is not material to ask what sort of ornaments they wore; many of these things, if they had not been in fashion, would have been ridiculed then as now. Their fashions differed much from those of our times, but human nature is the same. Wasting time and money, to the neglect of piety, charity, and even of justice, displease the Lord. Many professors at the present day, seem to think there is no harm in worldly finery; but were it not a great evil, would the Holy Spirit have taught the prophet to expose it so fully? The Jews being overcome, Jerusalem would be levelled with the ground; which is represented under the idea of a desolate female seated upon the earth. And when the Romans had destroyed Jerusalem, they struck a medal, on which was represented a woman sitting on the ground in a posture of grief. If sin be harboured within the walls, lamentation and mourning are near the gates.

The consequences of war (verse 1)

Henry observes that this opening verse continues the subject of chapter 3.

As disaster swept through the land, unmarried women—who faced social shame under the customs of the time—would depart from customary behavior and seek husbands for themselves.

This was one consequence of the war and devastation Isaiah foretold.

The Branch of the Lord and Zion's cleansing (verses 2–6)

Isaiah's promise concerns not only Christ's kingdom established in the apostolic age, but also its future enlargement as scattered Jews are gathered into the church.

Christ is called the Branch of the Lord because God's power plants him and causes him to flourish for divine praise.

The gospel is the Branch's fruit. All its blessings, spiritual graces and consolations spring from Christ.

It is called the fruit of the earth because its work appeared in this world and meets our needs in our present condition.

We show that we belong to true Israel when we see our greatest beauty in Christ and holiness, rather than merely possessing Israel's name.

Jerusalem's restoration and renewed fruitfulness would be a sign of this greater blessed age.

God keeps for himself a holy seed even when many who hold a visible place in Zion fall through unbelief.

When the Son of Man cleanses his kingdom, only those made holy will remain.

God's Providence may expose and remove sinners through judgment. But the Spirit of grace renews and converts.

He is the Spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind and convicting the conscience.

He is also the Spirit of burning, awakening holy affection and strengthening believers to pursue good with zeal.

Love for Christ and for souls, together with hatred of sin, moves believers to turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

Trials become a furnace that removes the dross from God's people. Through the Spirit's illuminating and powerful work, their sinful desires gradually lose their hold, and believers become more like the holy God.

The Lord protects his church and all who truly belong to it.

Gospel truth and appointed worship are the church's glory. Grace within a soul is that soul's glory, and God guards those who possess it.

Only the weary seek rest. Only those who recognize an approaching storm seek shelter.

Realizing that sin exposes us to divine displeasure, let us immediately take refuge in Jesus Christ and gratefully receive the protection he gives.

[Isa.4.1]
Chapter 4
The havoc occasioned by war. ( [Isa.4.1] Is. 4:1) The times of the Messiah. ( [Isa.4.2-Isa.4.6] Is. 4:2-6)
Verse 1 This first verse belongs to the third chapter. When the troubles should come upon the land, as the unmarried state was deemed reproachful among the Jews, these women would act contrary to common usage, and seek husbands for themselves.
[Isa.4.2-Isa.4.6]
Verses 2-6 Not only the setting forth Christ's kingdom in the times of the apostles, but its enlargement by gathering the dispersed Jews into the church, is foretold. Christ is called the Branch of the Lord, being planted by his power, and flourishing to his praise. The gospel is the fruit of the Branch of the Lord; all the graces and comforts of the gospel spring from Christ. It is called the fruit of the earth, because it sprang up in this world, and was suited for the present state. It will be good evidence that we are distinguished from those merely called Israel, if we are brought to see all beauty in Christ, and holiness. As a type of this blessed day, Jerusalem should again flourish as a branch, and be blessed with the fruits of the earth. God will keep for himself a holy seed. When most of those that have a place and a name in Zion, and in Jerusalem, shall be cut off by their unbelief, some shall be left. Those only that are holy shall be left, when the Son of man shall gather out of his kingdom every thing which offends. By the judgment of God's providence, sinners were destroyed and consumed; but by the Spirit of grace they are reformed and converted. The Spirit herein acts as a Spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind, convincing the conscience; also as a Spirit of burning, quickening and strengthening the affections, and making men zealously affected in a good work. An ardent love to Christ and souls, and zeal against sin, will carry men on with resolution in endeavours to turn away ungodliness from Jacob. Every affliction serves believers as a furnace, to purify them from dross; and the convincing, enlightening, and powerful influences of the Holy Spirit, gradually root out their lusts, and render them holy as He is holy. God will protect his church, and all that belong to it. Gospel truths and ordinances are the glory of the church. Grace in the soul is the glory of it; and those that have it are kept by the power of God. But only those who are weary will seek rest; only those who are convinced that a storm is approaching, will look for shelter. Affected with a deep sense of the Divine displeasure, to which we are exposed by sin, let us at once have recourse to Jesus Christ, and thankfully accept the refuge he affords.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe state and conduct of the Jewish nation.1–7The judgments which would come.8–23The executioners of these judgments.24–30
God's carefully tended vineyard (verses 1–7)

Jesus Christ is God's beloved Son and our beloved Savior.

The Lord's care for Israel is pictured through the tending of a vineyard.

One day we will answer to him for all the advantages and opportunities we have received.

He planted the finest vines, gave Israel an excellent law and instituted appropriate forms of worship.

The temple was like a vineyard's tower, where God gave signs of his presence. His altar, where sacrifices were offered, represented the appointed means of grace.

God expects fruit from people who receive such privileges.

Good intentions and promising beginnings are worth something, but they are insufficient by themselves. There must be genuine fruit: thoughts, desires, words and actions guided by the Spirit.

Instead, the vineyard produced wild grapes—the products of corrupted human nature.

Where God's grace does not bear fruit, sin will.

When people who profess faith misuse their privileges and reject grace, the responsibility is their own.

They may lose their distinct standing among God's people.

A vineyard left unpruned becomes overgrown with thorns. When errors and sinful habits are never corrected, the same thing happens to a community.

God may withdraw his Spirit from people who persistently resist him, or remove the preaching of the gospel from places that have long dishonored it.

Consider the contrast between the fruit he seeks and the fruit our hearts produce.

He seeks humility, gentleness, love, patience, freedom from worldly obsession, prayer and praise.

Sin produces pride, anger, discontent, malice, contempt for God, curses and irreverent speech.

May we bear fruit patiently and finally receive everlasting life.

Warnings against greed, pleasure and moral confusion (verses 8–23)

The Lord pronounces judgment on people who devote their hearts to wealth.

Owning a house and a field and buying another is not in itself sinful.

The fault lies in never recognizing that one has enough.

Greed is idolatry.

Many envy the prosperous person whom God calls miserable because of greed.

The Lord has many ways to empty even crowded cities. People who seek ultimate satisfaction in possessions will be disappointed.

He also warns those who live only for sensual pleasure.

Music is not wrong in itself, but becomes sinful when it diverts the heart from God.

People may continue pursuing pleasure even while divine judgments are unfolding around them.

Death lowers everyone, whether high or low.

In judging pride, God reveals both his power and his holiness.

Woe to those who deliberately pursue sinful desires, mock the Holy One of Israel and dare to challenge him.

They reverse the distinction between good and evil.

They prefer their own reasoning to God's revelation, and their personal schemes to his commands.

They treat profitable wrongdoing as prudent and duties requiring self-denial as foolish.

Drunkenness is no harmless pastime; it exposes the person to divine judgment.

Even judges may corrupt justice to protect their interests.

One sin frequently requires another sin to hide it.

The approaching instruments of judgment (verses 24–30)

Those who live in wickedness should not expect an easy life.

Sin weakens a nation's roots and destroys its blossoms—its strength and beauty.

When people reject God's word and law, they should not be surprised if he abandons them to judgment.

Under divine wrath, even mountains tremble and the powerful are afraid.

God can readily find instruments to punish people who continually provoke him.

Henry points to the Chaldeans, and later the Romans, as instruments used in the historical destruction of Judah and Jerusalem.

Those refusing to listen to God's warnings through his prophets would instead hear the threatening voices of their enemies.

They would find no refuge wherever they turned.

If God is displeased with us, no created source of comfort can finally make us secure.

Let us seek a well-founded assurance that, when every earthly support fails, God himself will remain the strength of our hearts and our portion forever.
classic_reading:
[Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7]
Chapter 5
The state and conduct of the Jewish nation. ( [Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7] Is. 5:1-7) The judgments which would come. ( [Isa.5.8-Isa.5.23] Is. 5:8-23) The executioners of these judgments. ( [Isa.5.24-Isa.5.30] Is. 5:24-30)
Verses 1-7 Christ is God's beloved Son, and our beloved Saviour. The care of the Lord over the church of Israel, is described by the management of a vineyard. The advantages of our situation will be brought into the account another day. He planted it with the choicest vines; gave them a most excellent law, instituted proper ordinances. The temple was a tower, where God gave tokens of his presence. He set up his altar, to which the sacrifices should be brought; all the means of grace are denoted thereby. God expects fruit from those that enjoy privileges. Good purposes and good beginnings are good things, but not enough; there must be vineyard fruit; thoughts and affections, words and actions, agreeable to the Spirit. It brought forth bad fruit. Wild grapes are the fruits of the corrupt nature. Where grace does not work, corruption will. But the wickedness of those that profess religion, and enjoy the means of grace, must be upon the sinners themselves. They shall no longer be a peculiar people. When errors and vice go without check or control, the vineyard is unpruned; then it will soon be grown over with thorns. This is often shown in the departure of God's Spirit from those who have long striven against him, and the removal of his gospel from places which have long been a reproach to it. The explanation is given. It is sad with a soul, when, instead of the grapes of humility, meekness, love, patience, and contempt of the world, for which God looks, there are the wild grapes of pride, passion, discontent, and malice, and contempt of God; instead of the grapes of praying and praising, the wild grapes of cursing and swearing. Let us bring forth fruit with patience, that in the end we may obtain everlasting life.
[Isa.5.8-Isa.5.23]
Verses 8-23 Here is a woe to those who set their hearts on the wealth of the world. Not that it is sinful for those who have a house and a field to purchase another; but the fault is, that they never know when they have enough. Covetousness is idolatry; and while many envy the prosperous, wretched man, the Lord denounces awful woes upon him. How applicable to many among us! God has many ways to empty the most populous cities. Those who set their hearts upon the world, will justly be disappointed. Here is woe to those who dote upon the pleasures and the delights of sense. The use of music is lawful; but when it draws away the heart from God, then it becomes a sin to us. God's judgments have seized them, but they will not disturb themselves in their pleasures. The judgments are declared. Let a man be ever so high, death will bring him low; ever so mean, death will bring him lower. The fruit of these judgments shall be, that God will be glorified as a God of power. Also, as a God that is holy; he shall be owned and declared to be so, in the righteous punishment of proud men. God promises that the attack will fail (verses 1–9)

Ungodly people are often punished through others who are just as wicked.

The people of Judah were terrified by the armies of Israel and Syria.

Having made God their enemy, they did not know how to find his favor again.

Isaiah was called to teach them confidence in God's protection, rather than fear of their enemies.

Ahaz regarded the attacking kings as powerful. The prophet dismissed them as the smoking ends of two burned-out torches.

The kingdoms of Syria and Israel were already nearing their end.

Worldly rulers may for a time accomplish the purposes God permits, bringing destruction to others. But when their work is complete, he can extinguish their power.

Their attack on Judah would fail because they had devised an evil plan that offended God.

Human beings make plans; God decides their outcome.

How foolish for rulers already close to ruin to plan the destruction of their neighbors!

Isaiah therefore urged the people to believe the Lord's promise. Faith is necessary to quiet the heart during severe trouble.

The sign of the promised Messiah (verses 10–16)

People who inwardly distrust God sometimes disguise that unbelief as reverence.

They refuse to trust his word yet claim they are unwilling to test him.

Isaiah rebuked Ahaz and his court for treating divine revelation so lightly.

Distrust greatly dishonors God. But human unbelief cannot cancel his promise.

The Lord himself would give a sign.

The Messiah was to be born from this people. Judah could not be completely destroyed before that blessing was fulfilled.

The promise points to a glorious birth and gives comfort through Christ, our relationship to him and our hope in him.

He would grow as other children did, eating ordinary food in his country. Yet unlike fallen children, he would always reject evil and choose good.

His birth would be accomplished by the Holy Spirit's power, but he would not need extraordinary food from angels.

Then Isaiah speaks of the nearer, swift defeat of Judah's two enemies.

Henry offers a possible reading of the immediate sign: before Shear-jashub, the prophet's young son present with him (Isaiah 7:3), grew three or four years older, the two hostile kings would no longer rule their forces.

This is presented as Henry's interpretation, not an identification of Shear-jashub with the promised Messiah.

Because God supplied the sign even after Ahaz had refused to ask, the prophecy could raise hope far beyond the immediate political crisis.

For believers awaiting the Messiah, that hope was a lasting comfort.

How thankful we should be that the Word became flesh! May we trust him, love him and follow his example.

The cost of relying on Assyria (verses 17–25)

People unwilling to believe God's promises should expect his warnings to become frighteningly real.

No one can escape his judgments.

The Lord can sweep away a nation's supports and use whatever instruments he chooses, repaying or dismissing them as he wills.

Judah's pleasant land would be transformed. Agriculture would cease, and former fields would become desolate.

What sorrow can sin not bring upon a people?

Those who neglect the great salvation place themselves in danger of every kind of misery.

If we continually remain unfruitful despite enjoying the means of grace, we should tremble at the warning that fruit may never grow from us again.

Isaiah was instructed to write on a large scroll or metal tablet words meaning “Hurry to the plunder; rush to the prey.”

They foretold how quickly the Assyrian army would arrive and seize enormous spoils.

Soon the wealth of Damascus and Samaria, cities that then appeared secure and powerful, would be carried away by Assyria.

The prophet appealed to the promised Messiah, who would one day appear in this land. Henry understands this appeal as resting on the Messiah's divine power to protect it in the meantime.

A gentle stream represents a mild, peaceable government. A raging flood pictures the overwhelming power of an invading conqueror and tyrant.

The invader's success is also described as a bird of prey spreading its wings across the land.

Those who reject Christ may call their rejection freedom, but they will discover it is the deepest slavery.

Yet no enemy can take a believer from Emmanuel's hand or deprive that person of the heavenly inheritance.

Isaiah challenged Judah's enemies: their plans would come to nothing, and their strength would be broken.

During trouble, we must guard against fears that lead us to dishonest or sinful methods of protecting ourselves.

Reverent fear of God protects us from the tormenting fear of human beings.

If we properly understood his majesty and power, we would see that our enemies' strength remains under his control.

The Lord is a sanctuary for those who trust him.

But to those who put their fear and hope in created things, he becomes a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.

If God's truth itself offends us, it will become the cause of our ruin.

The apostle applies this warning to those persisting in unbelief toward Christ's gospel (1 Peter 2:8).

Crucified Emmanuel offended unbelieving Jews and continues to offend many who call themselves Christians.

They regard preaching of the cross as foolishness and reject his teachings and commandments.

Isaiah foresaw a time when the Lord would hide his face, yet he resolved to continue waiting for God's return in mercy.

His children's names served as divinely given reminders, calling the people to consider God's message, even though they were not miraculous signs.

Unbelieving Israelites sought guidance from diviners, employing foolish and sinful practices.

Where should we turn if we wish to know God's mind and our duty?

To the law and the testimony.

There we discover what is good and what the Lord requires.

We must speak about divine things in words taught by the Holy Spirit and submit ourselves to their authority.

Those who consult spirits while neglecting God's word invite distress and darkness.

Leaving God means leaving the path of all true good.

A resentful heart punishes itself through its own bitterness.

People who curse God and turn away from his light will find their fears deepening, with no way of relief.

Those who deliberately close their eyes to Scripture may rightly be left in spiritual darkness.

All human troubles are small compared with the destruction awaiting people who abandon the words of Christ to pursue deception.

He promised deliverance from Assyria.

Henry records that some interpreters see a further application to the Jews' release from captivity and a greater deliverance from sin and Satan's tyranny.

He also considers the phrase “because of the anointing” in relation both to faithful Israelites possessing God's grace and to the Messiah, God's Anointed One.

Verses 28–34 describe prophetically Sennacherib's advance toward Jerusalem.

There the Lord, in whom Hezekiah trusted, cut down the invader's army as a forest is cut down.

The same divine care extends to Christ's church in every age.

Because of the anointing of the great Redeemer, the yoke of every power opposing Christ must finally be broken.

Those who share in the Holy Spirit's anointing can be assured of complete and eternal deliverance.
classic_reading:
[Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4]
Chapter 10
Woes against proud oppressors. ( [Isa.10.1-Isa.10.4] Is. 10:1-4) The Assyrian but an instrument in the hand of God for the punishment of his people. ( [Isa.10.5-Isa.10.19] Is. 10:5-19) The deliverance from him. ( [Isa.10.20-Isa.10.34] Is. 10:20-34)
Verses 1-4 These verses are to be joined with the foregoing chapter. Woe to the superior powers that devise and decree unrighteous decrees! And woe to the inferior officers that draw them up, and enter them on record! But what will sinners do? Whither will they flee?
[Isa.10.5-Isa.10.19]
Verses 5-19 See what a change sin made. The king of Assyria, in his pride, thought to act by his own will. The tyrants of the world are tools of Providence. God designs to correct his people for their hypocrisy, and bring them nearer to him; but is that Sennacherib's design? No; he designs to gratify his own covetousness and ambition. The Assyrian boasts what great things he has done to other nations, by his own policy and power. He knows not that it is God who makes him what he is, and puts the staff into his hand. He had done all this with ease; none moved the wing, or cried as birds do when their nests are rifled. Because he conquered Samaria, he thinks Jerusalem would fall of course. It was lamentable that Jerusalem should have set up graven images, and we cannot wonder that she was excelled in them by the heathen. But is it not equally foolish for Christians to emulate the people of the world in vanities, instead of keeping to things which are their special honour? For a tool to boast, or to strive against him that formed it, would not be more out of the way, than for Sennacherib to vaunt himself against Jehovah. When God brings his people into trouble, it is to bring sin to their remembrance, and humble them, and to awaken them to a sense of their duty; this must be the fruit, even the taking away of sin. When these points are gained by the affliction, it shall be removed in mercy. This attempt upon Zion and Jerusalem should come to nothing. God will be as a fire to consume the workers of iniquity, both soul and body. The desolation should be as when a standard-bearer fainteth, and those who follow are put to confusion. Who is able to stand before this great and holy Lord God?
[Isa.10.20-Isa.10.34]
Verses 20-34 By our afflictions we may learn not to make creatures our confidence. Those only can with comfort stay upon God, who return to him in truth, not in pretence and profession only. God will justly bring this wasting away on a provoking people, but will graciously set bounds to it. It is against the mind and will of God, that his people, whatever happens, should give way to fear. God's anger against his people is but for a moment; and when that is turned from us, we need not fear the fury of man. The rod with which he corrected his people, shall not only be laid aside, but thrown into the fire. To encourage God's people, the prophet puts them in mind of what God had formerly done against the enemies of his church. God's people shall be delivered from the Assyrians. Some think it looks to the deliverance of the Jews out of their captivity; and further yet, to the redemption of believers from the tyranny of sin and Satan. And this, "because of the anointing;" for his people Israel's sake, the believers among them that had received the unction of Divine grace. And for the sake of the Messiah, the Anointed of God. Here is, [Isa.10.28-Isa.10.34] Is. 10:28-34, a prophetical description of Sennacherib's march towards Jerusalem, when he threatened to destroy that city. Then the Lord, in whom Hezekiah trusted, cut down his army like the hewing of a forest. Let us apply what is here written, to like matters in other ages of the church of Christ. Because of the anointing of our great Redeemer, the yoke of every antichrist must be broken from off his church: and if our souls partake of the unction of the Holy Spirit, complete and eternal deliverances will be secured to us.
